[00:00] Imagine waking up one morning and the sun is gone.
[00:03] Not behind clouds. Gone.
[00:06] Just a pale, useless disc hanging in a sky the color of ash.
[00:09] And it stays like that, day after day, month after month.
[00:13] For eighteen months, the crops rot in the fields.
[00:16] Snow falls in summer.
[00:18] And somewhere far away, a mountain you have never heard of has torn itself apart, and you are the one paying the price.
[00:24] That year really happened, and it is coming up in this video.
[00:28] But it is not the only year humanity tried its hardest to die.
[00:32] Today, we are counting down the five worst years to be alive in human history.
[00:36] No war lists, no opinions.
[00:39] Just the years when being a living, breathing human was the most dangerous thing you could be.
[00:44] Number one is at the end, and honestly, it is worse than anything you are picturing right now.
[00:50] You live in Northern Europe, and you are a farmer, which means you are one good harvest away from starving every single year of your life.
[00:57] And then, in the spring, it starts raining.
[01:00] It rains all summer, it rains through the harvest, it rains into autumn, and it does not stop.
[01:06] Not for weeks, for years.
[01:09] The fields drown. The grain rots before it can be cut.
[01:12] Salt, the only way you can preserve meat, cannot be made because the fire will not burn and the brine will not dry.
[01:18] So even the food you saved, you lose.
[01:21] By winter, people are eating animals they would never normally touch.
[01:25] Horses, dogs, cats, then bark, then boiled leather.
[01:30] Historians call it the Great Famine.
[01:32] In some regions, up to a quarter of the population died, and here is the cruelest part:
[01:37] this was not plague, and it was not war.
[01:40] It was weather. There was no enemy to fight, no cure to find.
[01:44] You just watched the sky, and the sky did not care.
[01:47] And if you somehow survived 1315, congratulations.
[01:51] You now have a weakened body, an empty storehouse, and thirty-three years to wait until the next entry on this list finds you.
[01:58] Here is a year that most worst-year lists completely skip.
[02:02] For thousands of years, tens of millions of people built civilizations in the Americas, cities bigger and cleaner than anything in Europe at the time.
[02:11] Tenochtitlan, the capital of the Aztec Empire, had around 200,000 people.
[02:16] Bigger than London. Bigger than Paris.
[02:19] And then a single disease arrived on a single ship: smallpox.
[02:23] The people of the Americas had never encountered it, not once in ten thousand years.
[02:27] Zero immunity. Not weak immunity, none.
[02:30] It moved faster than any army ever could.
[02:33] Whole cities died before they ever saw a European soldier.
[02:36] In one year, the disease killed more people than every war in the region combined.
[02:41] Within a century, up to 90% of the population was gone.
[02:44] It was the largest demographic collapse in the history of our species.
[02:49] And the worst part for the people living through it was that no one knew what was happening.
[02:53] The disease arrived before the explanation did.
[02:57] Your family sickens, your neighbors sicken, and there is no reason: no poisoned well, no invading army, just the end of everything, one household at a time.
[03:07] If you were born in the Americas around 1520, you did not just live through a bad year. You lived through the end of your world.
[03:14] You probably saw this one coming, but stay with me, because the version you know is the polite version.
[03:20] The Black Death reaches England, France, and Italy, and it does not behave like a disease.
[03:25] It behaves like a predator.
[03:27] With a normal plague, you have time.
[03:29] Time to run, to quarantine, to hope.
[03:31] The Black Death gave you days, sometimes hours.
[03:35] One morning you feel fine. By evening, there is a swelling under your arm. By the third day, you are gone.
[03:41] In Florence, the writer Boccaccio watched it happen and wrote that people dropped dead in the street mid-sentence.
[03:47] Parents abandoned their sick children.
[03:49] Priests refused to give last rites because the priest himself would be dead by Friday.
[03:53] Cities ran out of graves, then they ran out of gravediggers, then they ran out of people to dig the next pit, and they just threw the bodies in from a distance.
[04:02] Half of Europe died in roughly five years.
[04:05] Half. Think about your street: every second house, empty.
[04:10] And here is what makes 1348 worse than the numbers say:
[04:14] nobody knew how it spread.
[04:16] Some thought it was bad air, some thought it was punishment.
[04:19] People fled the cities and carried the plague to the countryside.
[04:23] They gathered in churches to pray and infected each other.
[04:26] Every instinct you would have followed made it worse.
[04:29] There was no version of this year where you could make the right choice.
[04:32] There was only whether luck found you.
[04:35] Now jump forward. You would think modern times would be safe.
[04:38] You would be wrong.
[04:39] World War I is finally ending.
[04:41] People are in the streets celebrating.
[04:44] And in the middle of the celebration, a flu starts spreading.
[04:46] Except it does not behave like a flu.
[04:49] A normal flu kills the old and the very young.
[04:51] This one killed healthy people in their 20s and 30s.
[04:55] Their own immune systems overreacted and drowned their lungs from the inside.
[05:00] Some victims went from perfectly healthy to dead in 24 hours.
[05:04] Doctors would examine a patient in the morning and find them gone by evening.
[05:08] And the war made it perfect: millions of soldiers moving in packed trains and ships.
[05:13] And then the censorship: the countries fighting the war refused to report their outbreaks because you do not tell the enemy that your army is sick.
[05:21] So the world stayed quiet while the virus traveled.
[05:25] Only one country reported it freely, and that was neutral Spain.
[05:29] That is why we call it the Spanish flu.
[05:32] Spain was not the source. Spain was just the only one willing to say it out loud.
[05:37] In the end, the flu killed more people than the war it ended.
[05:40] Estimates run from 50 million to 100 million.
[05:44] And the darkest detail of all: for decades, almost nobody talked about it.
[05:48] The worst pandemic in modern history got a fraction of the history books that the war got.
[05:53] The lesson of 1918 is not just that disease can win, it is that silence can be just as deadly as the virus.
[06:01] Number one: the year that a leading historian has called, literally, the worst year to be alive.
[06:06] 536.
[06:07] It starts with the sun.
[06:10] Across Europe, the Middle East, and parts of Asia, a strange fog settles over the sky.
[06:15] The sun is there, but it gives no light and no heat, like looking at it through dirty water.
[06:20] The historian Procopius wrote that the sun shone without brightness, like the moon, for the entire year.
[06:26] The cause, we know now: one, or maybe two, massive volcanic eruptions threw so much ash and sulfur into the sky that the whole planet dimmed.
[06:35] The temperature drops. Crops fail from Ireland to China.
[06:39] Summer frost kills the grain. Famine spreads across three continents at once.
[06:44] And then, while humanity is weakened and starving, the plague shows up.
[06:49] The Plague of Justinian arrives a few years later and kills tens of millions.
[06:53] What is left of the Roman Empire never recovers.
[06:56] The late 530s kicked off one of the coldest decades in two thousand years.
[07:01] Here is why 536 beats every other year on this list:
[07:05] in 1348, you could flee.
[07:07] In 1918, medicine was at least trying.
[07:11] In 536, there was nothing.
[07:13] No enemy you could fight, no germ you could see, no season that would save you, because the seasons themselves had broken.
[07:20] The sky was wrong, and nobody alive knew why, or whether it would ever be right again.
[07:26] Imagine living that: not knowing if the sun was coming back.
[07:30] Five years, rain that never stopped.
[07:33] A world ended by one ship.
[07:35] A plague that moved faster than fear.
[07:37] A flu the world refused to talk about.
[07:39] And the year the sun went out.
[07:42] And here is the quiet, comfortable truth: you are watching this video in one of the safest times humans have ever lived.
[07:48] Right now, in this moment.
[07:51] So which of the five would you survive the longest?
[07:53] Be honest, tell me in the comments.
[07:56] And if you want the other side of this video, the best years to be alive in history, let me know.
[08:00] That one might surprise you even more.

gancho_0_30s.que_se_dice: Imagine waking up one morning and the sun is gone... That year really happened, and it is coming up in this video. But it is not the only year humanity tried its hardest to die.
gancho_0_30s.que_se_ve: Un personaje animado estilo stickman/dibujo 2D despierta en una choza, mira por la ventana y ve el sol desaparecido cubierto por cenizas; campos de cultivo pudriéndose, nieve en verano, un volcán en erupción y el personaje sosteniendo un libro titulado 'Worst Years'.

bloques.como_abre: Plantea una hipótesis inmersiva en segunda persona imaginando un año sin sol.
bloques.como_cierra_o_engancha_al_siguiente: Muestra la lista del 5 al 1 con el puesto 1 censurado y advierte que es peor de lo que imaginas.

bloques.tema: Puesto 5: El año 1315 y la Gran Hambruna
bloques.como_abre: Pone al espectador en la piel de un campesino del norte de Europa dependiente de la cosecha.
bloques.como_cierra_o_engancha_al_siguiente: Dice que si sobreviviste a 1315, te quedan 33 años para la siguiente catástrofe de la lista.

bloques.tema: Puesto 4: El año 1520 y la viruela en América
bloques.como_abre: Afirma que este es un año que casi todas las listas omiten por completo.
bloques.como_cierra_o_engancha_al_siguiente: Concluye que no fue un mal año sino el fin de su mundo, y da pie al puesto que todos esperan.

bloques.tema: Puesto 3: El año 1348 y la Peste Negra
bloques.como_abre: Anticipa que 'probablemente viste venir este' pero promete contar la versión cruda.
bloques.como_cierra_o_engancha_al_siguiente: Explica que no había elección correcta sino puro azar, y salta repentinamente a la modernidad.

bloques.tema: Puesto 2: El año 1918 y la Gripe Española
bloques.como_abre: Contrasta la falsa seguridad de la modernidad y el fin de la Primera Guerra Mundial.
bloques.como_cierra_o_engancha_al_siguiente: Deja la lección sobre el silencio institucional y anuncia directamente el puesto número uno.

bloques.tema: Puesto 1: El año 536, el peor año de la historia humana
bloques.como_abre: Cita a historiadores que lo denominan literalmente el peor año para estar vivo.
bloques.como_cierra_o_engancha_al_siguiente: Recapitula poéticamente los horrores de los 5 casos antes de pasar a la reflexión final.

bloques.tema: Cierre, reflexión y llamado a la acción
bloques.como_abre: Brinda una verdad reconfortante: vivimos en uno de los momentos más seguros de la humanidad.
bloques.como_cierra_o_engancha_al_siguiente: Pregunta cuál año soportarías más y promete un video sobre los mejores años de la historia.

cierre.que_hace: Reflexiona sobre el confort actual del espectador frente al pasado, resume las 5 tragedias, formula una pregunta de supervivencia e introduce la idea de un próximo video complementario.

visual.estilo: Ilustración digital 2D limpia tipo webcomic / animación vector minimalista con personajes de cabeza redonda y trazo negro grueso.
visual.personaje_recurrente: Monigote blanco minimalista con camiseta marrón y un pequeño corazón rojo en el pecho.
visual.textos_en_pantalla: Subtítulos centrados en la parte inferior; carteles estilizados con fechas (1315, 1520, 1348, 1918, 536), porcentajes, nombres de eventos y flechas explicativas.
visual.mapas_graficos_o_diagramas: Mapas de Europa y del mundo con flechas de propagación, líneas de tiempo horizontales, diagramas de balanzas de mortalidad y gráficas anatómicas de pulmones.

audio.voz: Voz masculina generada por IA (o locución humana hiperprocesada), tono narrativo sombrío, pausado y envolvente; aprox. 130-140 palabras/minuto.
audio.musica: Música ambiental cinemática, tensa, melancólica y de fondo continuo, que acentúa la sensación de peligro y misterio.
audio.efectos_de_sonido: Efectos sonoros puntuales y sutiles (viento, lluvia, pasos, clics de interruptor, estampados de censura, sonidos secos al aparecer textos).

tecnicas_de_retencion: Censura visual del puesto #1 en la lista para forzar la curiosidad (00:44)
Narración en segunda persona 'Tú eres un granjero...' para generar empatía inmediata (00:50)
Giro contraintuitivo: descartar guerras y enfocarse en el clima o enfermedades silenciosas (00:37)
Cliffhangers narrativos conectando un evento con el siguiente: '33 años para el próximo' (01:54)
Contraste brutal de escalas numéricas (90% de población, balanzas de muertos vs guerras) (02:36)
frases_cortas_de_ejemplo: Imagine waking up one morning and the sun is gone.
This was not plague, and it was not war. It was weather.
It moved faster than any army ever could.
analisis.por_que_creo_que_se_hizo_viral: Combina una narrativa inmersiva en segunda persona con un estilo visual simple pero muy expresivo, abordando hechos históricos aterradores desde una perspectiva humana y psicológica que hace valorar el presente al espectador.
